role.title: Senior Product Manager, AI feature
role.team: A product squad shipping a feature where a model drafts or decides on the user's behalf

outcomes.text: The AI feature is used for the job it was built for, without a rise in the errors users report
outcomes.measure: share of eligible tasks completed with the feature, read beside reported errors

outcomes.text: Every release of the feature is gated by an eval suite the squad owns
outcomes.measure: releases that met the agreed pass line before shipping, out of all releases

outcomes.text: Cost per task stays inside the agreed budget as usage grows
outcomes.measure: model and tool spend per task against the budget line, monthly

competencies.name: Outcome framing
competencies.description: Turns a request into a problem, a definition of good, non-goals and a line that says whether it worked.

anchors.1: Describes features to build; no measure of whether they worked.
anchors.2: Names a metric but not a target, a window or what it would trade off.
anchors.3: States the problem, a definition of good with a target and window, and at least one non-goal.
anchors.4: Does all of 3, names the counter-metric that would show the win is false, and says which of value, usability, feasibility and viability is the biggest risk.

competencies.name: Eval design
competencies.description: Writes evals that catch the failures that matter before a user does.

anchors.1: Relies on trying a few prompts by hand; no written cases.
anchors.2: Writes happy-path cases only, or cases with no pass rule.
anchors.3: Writes cases for the main failure modes, each with a pass rule, and sets a pass line for release.
anchors.4: Does all of 3, adds cases from real failure reports, and says how the suite stays honest as the model changes.

competencies.name: Cost judgment
competencies.description: Weighs cost per task against the value of the task.

anchors.2: Mentions cost but cannot estimate it per task.
anchors.3: Estimates cost per task as tokens per task and price per token, and compares it with the value of the task.
anchors.4: Does all of 3 and names the cheaper path (smaller model, caching, no model) and the quality it would trade.

competencies.name: Restraint: knowing when not to use a model
competencies.description: Keeps steps out of the model where rules, templates or a person are cheaper, safer or more accurate.

anchors.1: Uses a model for every step, including arithmetic and irreversible actions.
anchors.2: Accepts a non-model option only when prompted.
anchors.3: Unprompted, keeps at least one step out of the model and says why (accuracy, cost or liability).
anchors.4: Does all of 3 and sets the rule for when the step could move to a model later, with the evidence that would justify it.

competencies.name: Continuous discovery
competencies.description: Learns from users every week and tests the riskiest assumption before building.

anchors.2: Talks to users occasionally, after decisions.
anchors.3: Has a weekly habit of user contact and names the assumption each conversation tested.
anchors.4: Does all of 3 and can show a decision the evidence reversed.

stages.name: Work sample
stages.task: You get 40 anonymised examples of what the feature produced and what the user did with it. In 90 minutes, write a one-page recommendation on whether to widen the feature: the eval cases that would gate it, the cost per task, which steps should not use a model, and the assumption you would test with users first. AI tools are allowed and expected; say where you used them.

anchors.3: A definition of good with a target and window, and non-goals.
anchors.4: Does all of 3 and names the counter-metric and the rollback line.

anchors.2: Names an assumption but no test.

anchors.4: Does all of 3 and says what result would stop the work.

questions.text: Tell me about a launch you led that did not land. How did you know, and what did you change?
follow_ups: What was the measure, and when did you read it?

questions.text: Describe the last time something a user said changed what you shipped.
follow_ups: How often do you talk to users now?

questions.text: A leader asks for the AI feature to cover twice as many cases next quarter. How do you decide what good looks like?

stages.name: Structured interview: judgment in AI use

questions.text: Walk me through an eval suite you wrote or owned. What failure did it catch that a demo would have missed?
follow_ups: How did you set the pass line?

questions.text: The monthly model bill doubles while usage grows by half. What do you look at first?
follow_ups: What would you trade to bring it down?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you decided not to use a model for something a model could do.
follow_ups: What would have had to be true to use one?

questions.text: How do you find out which assumption behind an AI feature is most likely wrong?

steps: Each interviewer records every score, with written evidence, before the debrief starts. Scores recorded after it starts do not count.
Interviewers do not see each other's scores or discuss the candidate until the debrief starts.
The facilitator runs run.py score and shares the packet. Nobody states a view first.
For each flagged competency, the interviewers read their evidence aloud, lowest score first, and compare it with the anchors.
Scores do not change in the debrief. If an interviewer finds they misread an anchor, the decision note says so.
The hiring manager decides against the band and the evidence, and writes the decision note; check-note checks it before it is sent.
